title: Zero Array Transformation II
statement:
You get an array `nums` of non-negative integers and a list `queries`. Each entry `queries[i] = [l_i, r_i, val_i]` is an operation: every element of `nums` whose index lies between `l_i` and `r_i` (inclusive) may be lowered by any whole amount from `0` up to `val_i`, and that amount is picked separately for each of those indices.

The queries are used in their given order. Return the smallest `k >= 0` for which applying just the first `k` queries can leave every element of `nums` equal to `0` (`k = 0` means using no query at all). If even all of the queries together cannot do this, return `-1`.
notes:
## Intuition

Because each query lets every covered index drop by any amount up to `val`, the first `k` queries can zero index `i` exactly when the `val`s of those queries that cover `i` add up to at least `nums[i]`. So "can the first `k` queries do it?" is a yes/no test, and it is monotone: adding queries only adds coverage, so once the answer is yes it stays yes. That makes the smallest good `k` a target for binary search.

Simulating the queries one by one and stopping when everything reaches zero is correct but costs O(n · q), too slow when both are 10^5.

## Approach

1. `canZero(k)` builds a difference array `diff`: for each of the first `k` queries add `val` at `left` and subtract it at `right + 1`.
2. Sweep the indices keeping the running sum `cover`, the total decrease available at index `i`. If `cover < nums[i]` anywhere, the answer is no.
3. If even `canZero(queries.length)` fails, return `-1`.
4. Binary search `k` in `[low, high] = [0, queries.length]`: when `canZero(mid)` holds, keep `mid` as a candidate (`high = mid`); otherwise skip past it (`low = mid + 1`). Return `low`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 0, 2]`. With all three queries the coverage is `[2, 5, 2]`, enough everywhere, so an answer exists. Search `low = 0`, `high = 3`: `mid = 1` gives coverage `[1, 1, 1]`, short at index 0, so `low = 2`. `mid = 2` gives `[2, 2, 2]`, which is enough, so `high = 2`. Now `low = high = 2`, the answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O((n + q) log q): each check costs O(n + k) and the search makes O(log q) checks.
- Space: O(n) for `diff`.

## Pitfalls

- The answer can be `0` when `nums` is already all zeros, so the search starts at `0`, not `1`.
- Check the full set of queries first; without it the search would return `queries.length` for an impossible input.
- `diff` needs `n + 1` slots because a range ending at the last index writes to `right + 1 = n`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `canZero(k)` | whether the first `k` queries can zero every element |
| `diff` | difference array of the coverage from the first `k` queries |
| `left`, `right`, `val` | one query's range and its largest decrease |
| `cover` | total decrease available at index `i` |
| `low`, `high` | the binary search range for the answer |
| `mid` | the number of queries being tested |

narration.5: A difference array with one spare slot, so a range that ends at the last index can still close.
narration.6: Add in each of the first k queries.
narration.7: Unpack the query's range and the most it can lower each covered element.
narration.8: From index left onward, val more decrease is available...
narration.9: ...and from right + 1 onward it no longer applies.
narration.11: cover will hold the total decrease available at the current index.
narration.12: Sweep the indices from left to right.
narration.13: The running sum of diff is the coverage at index i.
narration.14: If the coverage cannot reach nums[i], these k queries are not enough.
narration.16: Every index can reach zero with these k queries.
narration.19: The answer lies between using no queries...
narration.21: If even every query together falls short, no k works, so return -1.

narration.23: Try the middle number of queries.
narration.24: Can the first mid queries zero the array?
narration.25: Yes: mid works, so the answer is mid or smaller.
narration.27: No: fewer queries cannot work either, so the answer is above mid.
narration.30: low is now the smallest k for which the check passes.
